title: Vulnerability Scanning
summary: Vulnerability Scanning is the recurring, mostly automated process of asking every reachable asset what known weaknesses it carries, then turning that answer into a ranked repair queue. The mechanism is a comparison: the scanner inventories software versions, exposed services, open ports, and configuration settings, then matches those observations against vulnerability feeds and benchmark rules. In real environments scanning runs in layers, because no single scan sees everything. Network scanners see listening services, authenticated host scans see installed packages and missing patches, container and image scanners see build layers, and application scanners see input handling. Cloud providers add agentless disk and snapshot analysis that reaches machines never exposed to the network. Evidence appears as scan reports, scan engine logs, credentialed scan success rates, and the ticket history that links a finding to a fix and a later clean rescan. The common misunderstandings are that a clean scan means a secure system, and that the tool finds everything. Coverage is the real problem: unauthenticated scans miss almost all local software, scans cannot see systems they cannot route to, and they say nothing about business logic faults or design flaws. Teams also drown when they treat every finding as urgent, rather than deciding which exposure is actually reachable from the internet and holds real data.

beginner.definition: Vulnerability scanning means using a tool to check your computers, servers, and programs for known weaknesses. It produces a list of problems and how serious they look. The list helps you decide what to fix first.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers look for the same easy weaknesses that a scanner does. They often find them first. Without scanning, nobody knows how many old systems are running in the corners of the network. Scanning turns a vague worry into a clear list of jobs. It also proves that a problem was really fixed, not just marked as done.
howItWorks: First build a list of everything you own, because a scanner can only check assets it knows about.
Point the scanner at those assets and let it check versions, open ports, and settings.
Use real credentials for host scans, so the tool can see installed software instead of just open doors.
Review the findings with the system owner, remove duplicates, and confirm which ones are genuine.
Rank the work by exposure and impact, then send fixes to the teams that own each system.
Rescan after the fix and close the ticket only when the finding disappears.
beginner.example: Think of a yearly safety check on a fleet of vans. A mechanic walks around each van and checks the brakes and lights. Then the mechanic writes a list. Some vans need work today and others can wait. The garage keeps the reports, and the manager checks each repair. Vulnerability scanning works the same way. The vans are your servers, and the check runs every week instead of every year.
takeaways: A scanner only finds problems on assets you have already listed, so inventory comes first.
Scans without credentials find far less, so fix authentication before trusting the results.
Close a finding only after a fresh scan proves the fix worked.

objectives: Explain what vulnerability scanning can and cannot detect in a real environment.
Describe the difference between authenticated and unauthenticated scan results.
Prioritise findings using exposure, exploitability, and business impact.
Explain how to verify that a reported vulnerability has actually been remediated.
Identify common causes of scanner blind spots and false positives.
